value: upper bound on sensitivity of 0.0045 C/s (peak cooling rate) in L1, L2 and early L3 larvae
method: in vivo calcium imaging (GCaMP6m in the primary cold sensor neurons, strain R11F02>GCaMP6m) during sine-wave temperature modulation, amplitude 0.05 to 1.0 C, period 60 s, offset 17 C; responses compared with the zero level expected from a non-responsive neuron
conditions: larvae of three developmental stages (L1, L2, early L3), stage responses indistinguishable at the lowest amplitude and all above zero; the lowest amplitude was the smallest sine wave the equipment could generate, so 0.0045 C/s is an upper bound on the threshold, not a measured threshold; about 10 animals for each of 15 conditions (Figure 6 caption); the paper names one species, 'the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster', in the Introduction as its model and elsewhere says 'Drosophila larva(e)'; Methods 2.1 lists the strains (wild-type Canton-S, R11F02>GCaMP6m, Ir25a2 mutants, Ir25a>TeTxLC and rescue) without a species name; species rank, grade m (one named species); larvae held by gentle cover-slip compression (Methods 2.6); 0.0045 C/s is the paper's printed peak cooling rate for A = 0.05 C (Section 3.4); A x 2pi/60 s gives about 0.0052 C/s, a difference the paper does not explain

source.authors: Anastasiia Evans, Anggie J. Ferrer, Erica Fradkov, Joseph W. Shomar, Josh Forer, Mason Klein
source.title: Temperature sensitivity and temperature response across development in the Drosophila larva

where: Results 3.5 (sensitivity at the sensory and behavioural levels); Methods (imaging)
quote: Thus, these measurements place an upper bound in sensitivity of 0.0045°C/s for L1, L2, and early L3 larva stages.
note: Calcium imaging, in vivo, larvae immobilised for imaging. Quote taken from a PDF read through WebFetch pieces and confirmed on a second fetch; the preceding sentence (not quoted) says the three stages' responses are indistinguishable and significantly above the zero level. Preceding Methods text gives the stimulus parameters.

value: L2 larvae turning rate at constant temperature (bin centred at 0 C/s) differed significantly from the rate at a cooling rate of -0.002 C/s
method: larvae tracked in an isotropic or linear thermal gradient arena on agar; trajectories split into bins of temperature change per time (dT/dt) and turning rates computed per bin; bin turning rates compared
conditions: L2 stage example shown as a bar graph (Figure 7C); gradient arena set linearly between 13 and 21 C on the agar gel, starting at 17 C; about 20 larvae placed near the centre per run; the +0.006 C/s warming bin also differed from adjacent bins; the paper's own conclusion is that L2 larvae are sensitive to cooling rates of at least that amount; the paper names one species, 'the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster', in the Introduction as its model and elsewhere says 'Drosophila larva(e)'; Methods 2.1 lists the strains (wild-type Canton-S, R11F02>GCaMP6m, Ir25a2 mutants, Ir25a>TeTxLC and rescue) without a species name; species rank, grade m (one named species); the Figure 7 legend treats the −0.002 C/s comparison as the behavioural upper bound on sensitivity, significance by bootstrapping; mid-L3 and especially late-L3 larvae showed reduced sensitivity (Section 3.5)

source.authors: Anastasiia Evans, Anggie J. Ferrer, Erica Fradkov, Joseph W. Shomar, Josh Forer, Mason Klein

source.title: Removal or component reversal of local geomagnetic field affects foraging orientation preference in migratory insect brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens

value: highest orientation preference to the north direction, where food had been placed in the training phase ('original food'), in the geomagnetic field
method: two-phase cross-tube assay in a Helmholtz coil system: phase 1, ten rice seedlings at the north arm end and adults released at the centre for about 10 h; phase 2, insects collected near the food moved to a new cross tube without food and arm choice recorded for 0.5 h; chi-square on the four-arm distribution with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests; four fields: local GMF, near-zero field (NZMF), horizontal component reversal and vertical component reversal
conditions: local GMF total intensity 52,487 +/- 841 nT, inclination 56.29 deg; no food in the test tube; north was the food direction in the training phase and was never changed; 12 replicates per magnetic field setup, total insects tested 511 +/- 69, N = 241, 87, 157, 132 insects across the four arms in the GMF; lamp 15 W (320-680 nm) as light source, coils covered by a shade cloth; the next sentence of the paper gives south 14%, west 25.40% and east 21.39% (all significantly lower, p < 0.001); under horizontal component reversal the insects still went mostly north, 'similar to that in GMF' (chi-square = 87.872, p < 0.001; Fig. 4 caption N = 191, 93, 122, 91), so the north choice did not follow the reversed horizontal component; food direction and magnetic north were not separated, and this is not a demonstrated compass heading; the Fig. 3 caption counts sum to 617 against the stated total 511 +/- 69
where: Results, Geomagnetic field (GMF), with north as the initial food direction; Results, horizontal component reversal (Fig. 4)
quote: In the GMF, N. lugens showed the highest preference of foraging orienting to the north direction with original food (χ2 = 108.48, p < 0.001).
note: Lab assay, adults within 48 h of emergence. Paper also reports that the preference disappears in the near-zero field (separate record) and under vertical component reversal, persists under horizontal component reversal and that IscA1 knockdown reduced it.

source.title: Removal or component reversal of local geomagnetic field affects foraging orientation preference in migratory insect brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens

value: no orientation preference in a near-zero magnetic field: north 25.46%, south 22.22%, west 27.55%, east 24.77% (chi-square p = 0.088)
method: two-phase cross-tube assay in a Helmholtz coil system: phase 1, ten rice seedlings at the north arm end and adults released at the centre for about 10 h; phase 2, insects collected near the food moved to a new cross tube without food and arm choice recorded for 0.5 h; chi-square on the four-arm distribution with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests; here in the NZMF
conditions: NZMF average intensity about 500 nT at the centre of a spherical space, against a GMF of 52,487 nT; N = 110, 96, 119, 107 insects across the four arms; 12 replicates per setup; same light and shade-cloth conditions as the GMF test; the paper reports the same loss of preference under vertical component reversal of the GMF (north 25.18%, south 21.74%, west 29.53%, east 23.55%, p = 0.102); vertical reversal N = 139, 120, 163, 130 (Fig. 4B); test tube without food, north the training food direction
quote: In the NZMF, however, N. lugens were relatively equally distributed and the percentage of individuals orienting to the north, south, west and east direction was 25.46%, 22.22%, 27.55% and 24.77%, respectively (χ2 = 10.261, p = 0.088) (Fig. 3B).
note: Null result in the near-zero field. The preference also disappeared under vertical component reversal but persisted under horizontal component reversal (chi-square = 87.872, p < 0.001), so removing the field or reversing its vertical component abolished the north preference; the paper does not show that an unaltered field is needed. A four-arm chi-square of 10.261 sits poorly with the printed p = 0.088 (9.371 with p = 0.102 for vertical reversal); the paper states no degrees of freedom.

source.authors: Manuela Carnaghi, Steven R. Belmain, Richard J. Hopkins, Frances M. Hawkes
source.title: Multimodal synergisms in host stimuli drive landing response in malaria mosquitoes

value: with host odour and a transparent target, more mosquitoes were caught at a target set at 35 C and 45 C than at 25 C
method: wind-tunnel landing assay on a heated target, factorial treatments of visual cue (transparent or black), host odour (present or absent) and target temperature (25, 35 or 45 C); landings compared across temperatures
conditions: Anopheles coluzzii (colony from Burkina Faso, printed as An. coluzzii), non-blood-fed females four to twelve days old; arena 25 +/- 2 C and 65 +/- 5% RH; twelve treatments in all; Table 1 mean landing counts (as read through the page reader, not the table itself) were 4.8 +/- 0.88 at 25 C, 13.3 +/- 1.41 at 35 C and 11.8 +/- 1.24 at 45 C for odour with the transparent target; the paper gives no heat effect when the target is black with odour, and concludes that a thermal cue does not increase landing when odour and visual cue are both present; without odour heat gave no increase (transparent 0.2, 0.4, 1.1; black 2.0, 1.7, 1.2 landings at 25, 35, 45 C); 35 and 45 C did not differ; at least ten replicates per treatment, 25 +/- 1 females each, 30 min, landings caught on an adhesive film over the target
where: Results, Interaction between thermal cue and other host-associated cues; Table 1
quote: A higher number of mosquitoes were caught in the treatment where the transparent target was set at 35 °C and 45 °C and was presented with host odour when compared to the same target at 25 °C.
note: Behaviour, lab wind tunnel. Heat acted with odour .

source.authors: Manuela Carnaghi, Steven R. Belmain, Richard J. Hopkins, Frances M. Hawkes
source.title: Multimodal synergisms in host stimuli drive landing response in malaria mosquitoes

value: no increase in landings at 35 C or 45 C compared with 25 C for a black target with host odour
method: wind-tunnel landing assay on a heated black target with host odour present, target at 25, 35 or 45 C
conditions: same assay, species and arena as the companion record (An. coluzzii, 25 +/- 2 C arena); visual cue black and odour present, so the thermal cue added nothing in this combination; the paper concludes that a thermal cue does not increase landing if host odour and visual cue are present; Table 1 means for black with odour 10.4 (+/- 1.77), 15.9 (+/- 1.05), 15.2 (+/- 1.00) at 25, 35, 45 C, higher but not significantly different
where: Results, Interaction between thermal cue and other host-associated cues
quote: Furthermore, the number of landings were not different in treatments where the black surface was set at either 35 °C or 45 °C and was presented with host odour compared to the respective treatment where the temperature was 25 °C.
note: Null result from the same paper as the positive record.
